chapter_note.about: Uncertain reasoning replaces true and false with probabilities. A Bayesian network draws the causes as arrows and stores a small table of chances at each variable, so the whole joint distribution is a product of table entries. The arrows also say which variables can be treated as independent, and the rules for reading them are chains, forks and colliders. To answer a question you either sum the joint over the hidden variables and normalise, which variable elimination does with less work, or you estimate by sampling. The exam asks for products of table entries, independence statements read off a graph, and which inference methods are exact.

chapter_note.simple: Real life is uncertain, so we describe it with chances. A Bayesian network is a picture of what causes what, with a small table of chances at each spot. To find the chance of a whole story, you read one number from each table and multiply them. The arrows also tell you what you can ignore: some things become unrelated once you know a third thing, and some become related when you learn a shared effect. To answer a question like 'how likely is rain, given a skid', you add up all the ways the unknown parts could be and then scale the answer so it adds to 1. When that is too much work, you estimate by simulation. In exam words: Bayesian networks, factorisation, d-separation, enumeration, variable elimination, sampling and the Markov blanket.

cards.title: Factorising a joint distribution
cards.simple: A Bayesian network is a map of what causes what. Each variable is a box, and arrows point from causes to effects. Every box carries a small table that says how likely it is, given only its direct causes. To find the chance of one full story, such as 'flu, fever, no cough', you read one number from each box's table and multiply them. A box with no causes just uses its own plain chance. If the story needs the value 0, you read the number for 1 and subtract it from 1. It is like working out the cost of a meal by taking one price from each section of a menu. In exam words: the joint distribution is the product of each variable's probability given its parents.
cards.idea: A Bayesian network is a directed graph with a small table for each variable. The table (**CPT**) gives the chance of that variable given its parents only. The chance of one full story is the product of one table entry per variable: **P(X1, …, Xn) = Π P(Xi | parents(Xi))**. A variable with no parents uses its plain prior. For a value of 0, read 1 minus the entry for 1.
cards.idea_full: A joint distribution over n yes-or-no variables has 2^n numbers, which is far too many to write down. A Bayesian network saves effort with one assumption: each variable depends directly only on its parents, the nodes with an arrow into it. Given its parents, a variable ignores everything that is not its descendant. Then the chance of a full story can be built one variable at a time: each variable contributes P(value | parent values), read from its own table. For a binary variable the table lists P(X=1 | …) for every combination of parent values, and P(X=0 | …) is 1 minus that. Multiply the contributions and you have the joint probability of the story. If you add the products over all stories, the total is 1, so the factorisation really is a joint distribution.
cards.definition:
$$P(X_1,\dots,X_n)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}P\big(X_i\mid \text{parents}(X_i)\big)$$

Symbols: Π means 'multiply over every variable'. parents(Xi) are the nodes with an arrow into Xi. A CPT (conditional probability table) lists P(Xi=1 | each combination of parent values). For a binary variable, P(Xi=0 | …) = 1 − P(Xi=1 | …).

A node with no parents has an empty condition, so its factor is just P(Xi).
cards.intuition_full: Picture telling the story in order, from causes to effects. First say whether the person has flu: that happens with chance 0.2. Given that, say whether they have a fever: the chance depends only on the flu, and here it is 0.9. Given the flu again, say whether they cough. Each sentence of the story has its own chance, and chances of a story told step by step multiply. That is the chain rule, trimmed by the arrows. Without the arrows, the cough would have to depend on the flu and the fever together, and the tables would grow. With the arrows, the fever is not consulted, because given the flu the two symptoms are treated as independent. So each table stays small. The price is that you must read the right row: the row that matches the values of the parents in the story.

example.setup: Flu F causes fever V and cough C (arrows F → V and F → C). P(F=1) = 0.2. P(V=1 | F=1) = 0.9 and P(V=1 | F=0) = 0.1. P(C=1 | F=1) = 0.7 and P(C=1 | F=0) = 0.2. Find P(F=1, V=1, C=0).

cards.title: Conditional independence and d-separation
cards.simple: There are three ways two things can be linked. In a chain, your alarm rings, so you wake, so you are late; if you already know whether you woke, the alarm adds nothing about being late. In a fork, one hidden cause such as a storm makes both the lights flicker and the dog bark; once you know about the storm, the flicker tells you nothing more about the barking. In a collider, two unrelated things both cause one effect, like a flat battery and an empty tank that can each stop the car. They are unrelated until you learn the car will not start. Then finding that the battery is fine makes the empty tank more likely. In exam words: observing the middle node of a chain or fork blocks the path, but observing a collider (or one of its descendants) opens it.
cards.idea: In a network, independence follows the arrows. Look at a path through a middle node B. In a **chain** (A → B → C) and a **fork** (A ← B → C), A and C are linked, and observing B **blocks** the path. In a **collider** (A → B ← C), A and C are unlinked, and observing B or any descendant of B **opens** the path. Two sets are d-separated by the evidence when every path between them is blocked.
cards.idea_full: The arrows tell you how information can flow. In a chain, a cause pushes information down to its effect: learn A and you learn something about C through B. If you already know B, the link from A is cut, because B carries everything A had to say. A fork is the same: a common cause B makes A and C look related, but once you know the cause the relation disappears. A collider behaves the other way round. A and C are separate causes of B and know nothing of each other. But once you see the effect B, the two causes compete to explain it: if one is ruled out, the other becomes more likely. That is called explaining away. It happens when B is observed, and also when any descendant of B is observed, since a descendant carries some news about B. d-separation is the rule that combines these three cases. X and Y are independent given Z if every path between them contains a blocked node. A path is blocked at a chain or fork node that is in Z, and at a collider that is not in Z and has no descendant in Z.
cards.definition:
$$X\perp Y\mid Z\ \text{ when every path between }X\text{ and }Y\text{ is blocked given }Z$$

A path is blocked by Z if it contains:
• a chain A → B → C or a fork A ← B → C whose middle node B is in Z, or
• a collider A → B ← C where neither B nor any descendant of B is in Z.

Symbols: ⟂ reads 'is independent of'. X ⟂ Y | Z reads 'X is independent of Y given Z'. With Z empty, nothing is observed.
cards.intuition_full: Imagine each path as a pipe that carries news between two variables. Chains and forks are open pipes by default. Observing the middle node is like shutting a valve in the middle. A collider is the opposite: the pipe is shut by default, because the two causes feed into the effect and no news passes between them. Observing the effect opens the valve. The reason is simple arithmetic. If W = U or V and you see W = 1, the case where both are 0 is gone. What is left ties U and V together: U = 0 forces V = 1. A descendant of W works too, because seeing a child of W is partial news about W, which partly rules out the case where both causes are off. To judge a statement, find every path, check each middle node, and say independent only if every path is shut.

example.setup: U and V are independent fair coins (P(U=1) = P(V=1) = 0.5). W is 1 when U or V is 1, so U → W ← V is a collider. Show that U and V are independent, but become dependent once W = 1 is observed.
steps: Nothing observed. The four (U, V) combinations each have chance 0.25. P(U=1, V=1) = 0.25 = 0.5 × 0.5, so U and V are independent.
Observe W = 1. The combination (0, 0) would give W = 0, so it is ruled out.
The three left have 0.25 each, total 0.75. Rescale: 0.25 ÷ 0.75 = 0.333 each.
P(U=1 | W=1) = 0.333 + 0.333 = 0.667 and P(V=1 | W=1) = 0.667. Their product is 0.667 × 0.667 = 0.444. But P(U=1, V=1 | W=1) = 0.333. Not equal, so U and V are dependent given W.
Explaining away: if we also learn U = 0, then V must be 1. Observing the collider opened the path.
example.answer: U and V are independent a priori and dependent given W = 1.

examples.setup: Edges: P → Q, Q → R, S → R, R → T, S → U. Which statement is FALSE? (A) P ⟂ S. (B) P ⟂ S | T. (C) P ⟂ T | Q. (D) Q ⟂ U | S.
steps: (A) The only path from P to S is P → Q → R ← S. R is a collider and nothing is observed, so the path is blocked. P ⟂ S is true.
(B) Now T is observed. T is a child of the collider R, so it opens the collider. The path P → Q → R ← S is open. P and S are dependent, so (B) is false.
(C) The only path from P to T is P → Q → R → T. Q is a chain node and is observed, so the path is blocked. True.
(D) The only path from Q to U is Q → R ← S → U. R is an unobserved collider (blocked), and S is an observed fork node (blocked). True.
The false statement is (B). The trap is that a descendant of the collider opens it just like the collider itself.
examples.answer: (B) is false.

examples.setup: Edges: B → A, E → A, A → J (burglary, earthquake, alarm, John's call). Which of B ⟂ E, B ⟂ E | A, B ⟂ E | J, B ⟂ J | A are true?
steps: B and E meet at the collider A. With nothing observed the path is blocked: B ⟂ E is true.
Observe A: the collider opens, so B and E are dependent. B ⟂ E | A is false. (If the alarm rang and an earthquake happened, a burglary is less likely.)
Observe J instead. J is a child of the collider A, so it also opens the path: B ⟂ E | J is false.
B ⟂ J | A: the path is B → A → J, a chain through the observed node A. It is blocked. True.
examples.answer: True: B ⟂ E and B ⟂ J | A. False: B ⟂ E | A and B ⟂ E | J.

cards.title: CPTs and parameter counting
cards.simple: Say a student picks one of 3 clubs, and the second choice depends on the first. You do not store every pair of choices in one giant table. You store, for each first club, how likely each second choice is. A network keeps one such small table for each variable. Each row of a table adds up to 1, so the last number in a row is not free: it is whatever is left. Count the free numbers in all the small tables and compare with the one giant table. The network needs far fewer. In exam words: a node needs (number of parent combinations) × (own values − 1) free numbers, and the network total is the sum over nodes.
cards.idea: A **CPT** has one row for each combination of parent values, and each row must add to 1. So a node with v values needs **(v − 1)** free numbers per row. For a binary node with k binary parents that is **2^k** numbers. Add these up over all nodes to get the network's count. It is usually far smaller than the **2^n − 1** numbers of the full joint table.
cards.idea_full: Counting parameters tells you how compact a network is. For each node, count the rows of its CPT: that is the product of the number of values of its parents, or 1 if it has none. In each row the chances add to 1, so a node with v values has only v − 1 free numbers per row, because the last one is fixed by the others. Multiply rows by (v − 1) and you have the node's count. For a binary node with k binary parents the rows are 2^k and each has one free number, so the count is 2^k. The network's total is the sum over its nodes. The full joint over n binary variables has 2^n cells that add to 1, so 2^n − 1 free numbers. A sparse network, where each node has few parents, needs far fewer. That saving is the reason Bayesian networks are practical.
cards.definition:
$$\text{free numbers of node }X=\Big(\prod_{U\in\text{parents}(X)}|U|\Big)\times(|X|-1)$$

Symbols: |X| is the number of values of X. For a node with no parents the product is 1. The network total is the sum of this over all nodes. The full joint table has (product of all |Xi|) − 1 free numbers.

For binary variables: a node with k parents needs 2^k numbers, a root needs 1, and the full joint of n variables needs 2^n − 1.
cards.intuition_full: Think of each CPT as a set of dials. A row is a set of dials that must add to 100%, like splitting a budget across the values. If you set all but one dial, the last is forced, so it is not a free choice. Free numbers are the dials you can really turn. A node with many parents has many rows, so many sets of dials. That is why the number of parents matters so much: each extra binary parent doubles the rows. A node with 4 binary parents needs 16 numbers, and with 10 parents it needs 1024. The full joint table is a single node with every other variable as a parent, which is why it grows as 2^n. The network's savings come from each node paying only for its own parents.

example.setup: A network has edges A → B → C. A has 3 values, B has 2 values and C has 4 values. How many free numbers do the CPTs need? How many does the full joint table need?
steps: Each CPT has one row for every combination of parent values and one column for each value of the node. Every row adds to 1, so the last number in a row is not free.
A has no parent: 1 row of 3 numbers, and 3 − 1 = 2 are free.
B has parent A with 3 values: 3 rows. Each row has 2 numbers, so 2 − 1 = 1 is free per row. 3 × 1 = 3.
C has parent B with 2 values: 2 rows. Each row has 4 numbers, so 4 − 1 = 3 are free per row. 2 × 3 = 6.
Network total: 2 + 3 + 6 = 11. Full joint: 3 × 2 × 4 = 24 cells, so 24 − 1 = 23 free numbers.
example.answer: The network needs 11 free numbers. The full joint needs 23.

cards.what_full:
Counting parameters tells you how compact a network is. For each node, count the rows of its CPT: that is the product of the number of values of its parents, or 1 if it has none. In each row the chances add to 1, so a node with v values has only v − 1 free numbers per row, because the last one is fixed by the others. Multiply rows by (v − 1) and you have the node's count. For a binary node with k binary parents the rows are 2^k and each has one free number, so the count is 2^k. The network's total is the sum over its nodes. The full joint over n binary variables has 2^n cells that add to 1, so 2^n − 1 free numbers. A sparse network, where each node has few parents, needs far fewer. That saving is the reason Bayesian networks are practical.

$$\text{free numbers of node }X=\Big(\prod_{U\in\text{parents}(X)}|U|\Big)\times(|X|-1)$$

Symbols: |X| is the number of values of X. For a node with no parents the product is 1. The network total is the sum of this over all nodes. The full joint table has (product of all |Xi|) − 1 free numbers.

For binary variables: a node with k parents needs 2^k numbers, a root needs 1, and the full joint of n variables needs 2^n − 1.

2. A has no parent: 1 row of 3 numbers, and 3 − 1 = 2 are free.
3. B has parent A with 3 values: 3 rows. Each row has 2 numbers, so 2 − 1 = 1 is free per row. 3 × 1 = 3.
4. C has parent B with 2 values: 2 rows. Each row has 4 numbers, so 4 − 1 = 3 are free per row. 2 × 3 = 6.
5. Network total: 2 + 3 + 6 = 11. Full joint: 3 × 2 × 4 = 24 cells, so 24 − 1 = 23 free numbers.

cards.title: Inference by enumeration
cards.simple: You hear that a car skidded, and you want to know whether it had rained. You never checked whether the road was wet, so you think through both cases for the road. For each answer to 'did it rain?', you add up the chance of every way the road could have been, together with the skid. A wet road makes a skid more likely, and rain makes a wet road more likely, so rain gets a large total. But even without rain the road could be wet. The two totals do not add up to 1, so they are not chances yet. You scale them until they do. In exam words: enumeration sums the joint over the hidden variables and then normalises, P(Q | e) = α Σ P(Q, e, h).
cards.idea: To answer 'what is the chance of Q given the evidence e', add up the joint probability of every full story that matches. Fix a value of Q and the evidence, **sum over the hidden variables** (those that are neither the query nor the evidence), and do this for each value of Q. The totals are not yet probabilities, so **normalise**: divide each by their sum.
cards.idea_full: Enumeration is exact inference with no tricks. Every full story has a joint probability, which you can compute by multiplying CPT entries (card 1). The evidence fixes some of the variables. The query is the variable you want. The rest are hidden, and since you do not know their values you must consider all of them. For one value of Q, the probability of Q and the evidence is the sum of the joint over every combination of hidden values. Do this for every value of Q. The result for each value is P(Q=q, e), a joint probability of the query and the evidence. A conditional must add up to 1 over q, and these totals add up to P(e). So divide each by that sum. In formulas, P(Q | e) = α Σ P(Q, e, h), where α is 1 divided by the sum of the totals. The cost grows with the number of hidden variables, which is why the next card shows a smarter order of working.
cards.definition:
$$P(Q\mid e)=\alpha\sum_{h}P(Q,e,h),\qquad \alpha=\frac{1}{\sum_{q}\sum_{h}P(q,e,h)}$$

Symbols: Q is the query variable. e is the evidence, the observed values. h ranges over all combinations of values of the hidden variables. P(Q, e, h) is the joint probability, a product of CPT entries. α is the normalising constant.

Procedure: for each value q of Q, add up P(q, e, h) over all h. Then divide each total by the sum of the totals.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the joint distribution as a long list of stories with their chances. The evidence is a filter: keep only the stories that agree with what you saw. Among the survivors, group the stories by the value of the query and add up the chances in each group. The groups are in the right proportion to each other, but their sizes add up to less than 1, because you threw away the stories that disagreed with the evidence. Dividing by the total puts them back on a scale that adds to 1. That is all that conditioning ever is: filter, group, add, rescale. The hidden variables are what you sum over inside each group. You do not care which value they took, only that the story agrees with the evidence, so you add all of them in.

cards.title: Variable elimination
cards.simple: Enumeration repeats a lot of arithmetic. Imagine working out the results of a four-round quiz game. Instead of listing every full path, you squash the last round into a small table, then squash the next round using that table, and so on. Each piece of arithmetic is done once and reused. That is variable elimination: pick a hidden variable, multiply the tables that mention it, add over its values to remove it, and keep the small new table. At the end one table is left for your question, and you scale it so it adds up to 1. A smart order keeps the tables small. In exam words: variable elimination multiplies the factors that mention a variable, sums it out, repeats, then normalises. It is exact, and its cost depends on the largest factor.
cards.idea: **Variable elimination** gives the same answer as enumeration with less repeated work. Pick a hidden variable, **multiply** the tables (factors) that mention it, and **sum it out** to leave one smaller factor. Repeat for each hidden variable, then multiply what is left and normalise. It is exact. Its cost is set by the size of the largest factor, which depends on the order of elimination.
cards.idea_full: Enumeration multiplies a long product and sums it over all combinations of the hidden variables. But many terms share parts of the product. Variable elimination pulls out the shared parts. The useful fact is that a factor which does not mention a variable can be moved outside the sum over that variable. So to eliminate Z, you only multiply the factors that contain Z, add over the values of Z, and obtain a new factor over the remaining variables of those factors. That new factor replaces the old ones. Do this for every hidden variable, apply the evidence at the start so that observed variables do not appear in the factors, then multiply what remains, which is a factor over the query alone, and normalise. The answer is exact, identical to enumeration. The work depends on the largest factor created, because a factor over k binary variables has 2^k entries. Different orders of elimination can give very different sizes.
cards.definition:
$$f_{\text{new}}(\text{rest})=\sum_{x}\ \prod_{f\ni X} f(x,\text{rest})$$

Symbols: a factor is a table of numbers over some variables. To eliminate X: multiply all the factors that contain X, then add the product over every value of X. The result is a new factor without X. Evidence is applied first: only the rows that agree with the evidence are kept.

Size of a factor: the product of the numbers of values of its variables (2^k for k binary variables). The cost of the method is set by the largest factor.
cards.intuition_full: Think of a long multiplication like a × b × c + a × b × d. You can write it as a × b × (c + d), doing the shared part once. Variable elimination does this systematically. In a chain X → Y → Z → W, enumeration would add up four separate terms for each x. Elimination first squashes Z and W into a small table over Y, then squashes Y into a table over X. Each squash is one small sum, so the work grows with the length of the chain instead of exponentially. The order matters because it decides which variables are tangled together in the same product. Eliminating a variable that is connected to many others creates a large new factor, like taking a central hub out of a network and leaving a tangle of cross links behind.

steps: Eliminate A. Factors with A: P(A), P(B | A), P(C | A). The product covers {A, B, C}: 2^3 = 8 entries. Sum out A to get f1(B, C).
Eliminate B. Factors with B: f1(B, C) and P(D | B). The product covers {B, C, D}: 8 entries. New factor f2(C, D).
Eliminate C. Factors with C: f2(C, D) and P(E | C). The product covers {C, D, E}: 8 entries. New factor f3(D, E).
Eliminate D. Factors with D: f3(D, E) and P(F | D, E). The product covers {D, E, F}: 8 entries. New factor f4(E, F).
Eliminate E. Only f4(E, F), with 4 entries. The result is a factor over F.
The largest product has 8 entries.
examples.answer: 8 entries.

examples.setup: Same factors as in the gate example, but eliminate D first, then A, B, C, E. How does the cost change, and does the answer change?
steps: Eliminate D first. Factors with D: P(D | B) and P(F | D, E). The product covers {B, D, E, F}: 2^4 = 16 entries. Sum out D to get f(B, E, F), which has 8 entries.
Eliminate A. Factors with A: P(A), P(B | A), P(C | A). The product covers {A, B, C}: 8 entries. New factor g(B, C).
Eliminate B. Factors with B: g(B, C) and f(B, E, F). The product covers {B, C, E, F}: 16 entries.
So the largest factor now has 16 entries, twice as many as the 8 of the first order.
The final answer P(F) is the same for both orders. Only the work differs.
examples.answer: The largest factor grows from 8 to 16 entries. The answer P(F) does not change.

cards.title: Sampling methods
cards.simple: Sometimes the exact sum is too big, so you estimate by simulation, like asking a few voters to guess an election result. In rejection sampling you play out the whole story many times and throw away every run that does not match what you saw. It wastes a lot if what you saw is rare. In likelihood weighting you do not throw runs away: you set the things you saw to what you saw, play out the rest, and give each run a score for how well it fits. In Gibbs sampling you start with any full story and keep changing one thing at a time, each time looking only at the things around it. All of these are estimates, so they are approximate, while enumeration and variable elimination are exact. In exam words: rejection sampling, likelihood weighting and Gibbs sampling are approximate, and variable elimination is exact.
cards.idea: When exact inference is too costly, estimate by **sampling**. **Rejection sampling** draws full samples from the network and throws away those that disagree with the evidence. **Likelihood weighting** fixes the evidence and gives each sample a **weight**: the product of the evidence CPT entries. **Gibbs sampling** repeatedly resamples one non-evidence variable given its Markov blanket. All three are **approximate**. Enumeration and variable elimination are exact.
cards.idea_full: Sampling estimates a probability by counting. In rejection sampling you draw a full assignment from the network, going from causes to effects. If it disagrees with the evidence, discard it. The estimate of P(Q=q | e) is the share of the kept samples with Q=q. If the evidence is unlikely, almost every sample is thrown away. Likelihood weighting fixes this by never sampling the evidence variables. They are set to their observed values, the other variables are sampled in order, and each sample gets a weight equal to the product of P(evidence value | its sampled parents). The estimate is the weighted share: the total weight of samples with Q=q, divided by the total weight. Gibbs sampling is different: it keeps one current full assignment and repeatedly picks a non-evidence variable, resamples it from P(variable | its Markov blanket), and records the state. Its samples are correlated and converge to the right distribution in the long run. None of these give the exact answer after a finite number of samples. Enumeration and variable elimination do.

Rejection sampling: estimate = (kept samples with Q = q) ÷ (kept samples). A sample is kept only if it agrees with all the evidence.

Gibbs sampling: resample X from P(X | Markov blanket of X), which is proportional to P(X | parents) × the product over children of P(child | its parents).

Exact: enumeration, variable elimination. Approximate: rejection sampling, likelihood weighting, Gibbs sampling.
cards.intuition_full: Imagine you want the fraction of left-handed people in a town but cannot ask everyone. You sample some people and count. That is a sampling estimate: more people give a better estimate, but never certainty. Conditioning adds a twist. If you only care about left-handed people who play tennis, a plain sample wastes most of its effort on people who do not play tennis. Rejection sampling accepts that waste. Likelihood weighting avoids it by only generating tennis players, but then each person counts for more or less, depending on how likely that kind of person is to play tennis. That count is the weight. Gibbs sampling takes a third route: it starts from a plausible tennis player and keeps making small changes to their other traits, each change drawn from what is typical given the neighbours.

cards.title: Probability toolkit
cards.simple: Three tools do most of the work in these questions. The first is adding up: if you know the chance of every combination, add up the combinations you do not care about to get the chance of the thing you do care about, like adding the rows of a table. The second is zooming in: if you are told one thing happened, look only at that part of the table and rescale it so it adds up to 1. The third is flipping: Bayes' rule turns 'the chance of a positive test when ill' into 'the chance of being ill after a positive test', using how common the illness is. A last idea is 'independent given Z': once you know Z, learning Y tells you nothing new about X. In exam words: marginalisation, Bayes' rule, and conditional independence, P(X | Y, Z) = P(X | Z).
cards.idea: Three tools solve most network questions. **Marginalisation** adds the joint over the variables you do not need. **Conditioning** keeps only the cells that match what you know and rescales them. **Bayes' rule** flips a conditional: P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A) / P(B). Conditional independence means that once Z is known, Y tells you nothing more about X: P(X | Y, Z) = P(X | Z).
cards.idea_full: A joint table lists the chance of every combination. Marginalising sums out a variable: the chance of F=1 is the sum of the chances of (F=1, T=1) and (F=1, T=0). Conditioning restricts to what you know: given T=1, only the T=1 column matters, and you divide by that column's total so that the column adds to 1. Bayes' rule is that division written with other quantities. P(F=1 | T=1) is P(F=1, T=1) divided by P(T=1), and P(F=1, T=1) can also be written P(T=1 | F=1) P(F=1). So P(F=1 | T=1) = P(T=1 | F=1) P(F=1) / P(T=1). This is how you turn a test's accuracy into the chance of being ill. The base rate P(F=1) is what links the two directions. Conditional independence is checked with a product: X and Y are independent given Z when P(X, Y | z) = P(X | z) P(Y | z) for every value z of Z. It must hold for all z, not just one.
cards.definition:
$$P(X)=\sum_{y}P(X,y)\qquad P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}\qquad X\perp Y\mid Z\iff P(X\mid Y,Z)=P(X\mid Z)$$

Symbols: Σy adds over every value of y. P(A | B) is the chance of A when B is known. The bar reads 'given'. P(B) in the denominator is itself found by marginalising: P(B) = Σ P(B | A) P(A).

Conditional independence also means P(X, Y | Z) = P(X | Z) P(Y | Z) for every value of Z.
cards.intuition_full: Treat the joint table as a map of the whole population, where each cell is the share of people in that group. Marginalising is zooming out: forget one attribute and merge the groups. Conditioning is zooming in on a part of the map: if you are told the test was positive, you are now only among the positive people, and the question becomes what share of those are ill. That is the cell divided by the column total. Bayes' rule is a way to do this when you only know the shares the other way round: you know what share of ill people test positive, and you want the share of positive people who are ill. The answer depends on how many ill people there are at all. If illness is rare, most positives are healthy people who tested positive by mistake, even with an accurate test.

cards.title: Markov blanket
cards.simple: Imagine you want to predict how one person at a party will behave, and you can ask a few others. Whom do you need? The people who influence them (their parents), the people they influence (their children), and the partners of those children, because a child's behaviour depends on both parents. Once you have heard from all of these, nobody else at the party adds anything: not the grandparents, not the grandchildren. That group is the Markov blanket. In exam words: the Markov blanket of a node is its parents, its children and its children's other parents. Given the blanket, the node is independent of every other node.
cards.idea: The **Markov blanket** of a node is the smallest set that shields it from the rest of the network: its **parents**, its **children**, and its children's **other parents**. Given the blanket, the node is independent of every other variable. This is what Gibbs sampling uses: to resample a node you only need to look at its blanket.
cards.idea_full: Why these three groups? The node's own table involves its parents, so they are needed. Each child's table involves the node, so the children are needed. But a child's table also involves the child's other parents. If you want P(node | everything else), the children's tables are part of it, and those tables contain the co-parents. So the co-parents have to be known too. Anything further away, such as grandparents or grandchildren, only influences the node through the blanket, so once the blanket is known they add nothing. That is the same as saying the blanket d-separates the node from the rest (card 2). The practical formula is P(X | all others) proportional to P(X | parents of X) times the product over the children of P(child | its parents). Every other factor in the joint product does not mention X, so it cancels when you normalise. That is why Gibbs sampling can update one variable using only the blanket.
cards.definition:
$$\text{MB}(X)=\text{parents}(X)\ \cup\ \text{children}(X)\ \cup\ \text{other parents of the children of }X$$

Count each node once, even if it is a co-parent of several children. X itself is not in its own blanket.

Given MB(X), X is independent of all the other variables. In formulas: P(X | all others) is proportional to P(X | parents of X) × the product over children c of P(c | parents of c).
cards.intuition_full: Picture the joint probability as a long product of tables, one for each node. If you freeze everything except X, then only the tables that mention X change as X changes. Those are X's own table and the table of each child, since a child's table has X among its inputs. All the other tables are constants, and they cancel when you rescale. So to know X's conditional distribution, you need to know the values mentioned in those tables: X's parents, X's children, and the other parents of each child. Nothing else appears. Grandparents appear only in the parents' tables, which do not contain X, so they cancel. Grandchildren appear in the children's children's tables, which do not contain X either. This is why the blanket is such a small set compared with the whole network.

cards.what_full:
Why these three groups? The node's own table involves its parents, so they are needed. Each child's table involves the node, so the children are needed. But a child's table also involves the child's other parents. If you want P(node | everything else), the children's tables are part of it, and those tables contain the co-parents. So the co-parents have to be known too. Anything further away, such as grandparents or grandchildren, only influences the node through the blanket, so once the blanket is known they add nothing. That is the same as saying the blanket d-separates the node from the rest (card 2). The practical formula is P(X | all others) proportional to P(X | parents of X) times the product over the children of P(child | its parents). Every other factor in the joint product does not mention X, so it cancels when you normalise. That is why Gibbs sampling can update one variable using only the blanket.

scenes.title: Joint probability as one table entry per node

steps.caption: Flu F causes fever V and cough C. Each node has a small table of chances (CPT), given its parents only. We want one full story: F = 1, V = 1, C = 0 (flu, fever, no cough).
F has no parent, so we use its plain prior: P(F=1) = 0.2.
V has parent F, and F = 1 in our story. Read the F = 1 row: P(V=1 | F=1) = 0.9.
C has parent F, and our story has C = 0. The table gives C = 1, so take the complement: 1 − P(C=1 | F=1) = 1 − 0.7 = 0.3.
Multiply one entry per variable: 0.2 × 0.9 = 0.18, then 0.18 × 0.3 = 0.054.

scenes.title: A collider: observing W links U and V

steps.caption: U and V are two fair coins that do not affect each other. W = 1 when U or V is 1. Each of the four (U, V) combinations has chance 0.25, and P(U=1, V=1) = 0.25 = 0.5 × 0.5. So U and V are independent.

set.text: nothing observed: U and V independent

steps.caption: Now we observe W = 1. The combination U = 0, V = 0 would give W = 0, so it is ruled out.
The three remaining combinations had 0.25 each, 0.75 in total. Rescale them to add to 1: 0.25 ÷ 0.75 = 0.333 each.

Test independence given W = 1. P(U=1 | W=1) = 0.333 + 0.333 = 0.667, and P(V=1 | W=1) = 0.667. If they were independent, P(U=1, V=1 | W=1) would be 0.667 × 0.667 = 0.444. It is 0.333. So U and V are now dependent.
This is explaining away. If we also learn U = 0, then V must be 1: P(V=1 | W=1, U=0) = 1. Observing the collider W made U and V depend on each other.

set.text: learn U = 0  then  V = 1 for sure

scenes.title: Counting the free numbers in the tables of A → B → C

steps.caption: A has 3 values, B has 2 and C has 4, with edges A → B → C. Each CPT has one row for every combination of parent values and one column for each value of the node. Every cell holds a probability p.
P(A) is one row of 3 numbers that must add to 1. The last one is whatever is left, so only 3 − 1 = 2 are free.
P(B | A) has one row for each of the 3 values of A. Each row has 2 numbers that add to 1, so 1 is free per row: 3 × 1 = 3.
P(C | B) has one row for each of the 2 values of B. Each row has 4 numbers that add to 1, so 3 are free per row: 2 × 3 = 6.
Add up the free numbers: 2 + 3 + 6 = 11. The full joint table has 3 × 2 × 4 = 24 cells, so 23 free numbers. The network needs less than half.

scenes.title: Enumeration: sum out the hidden variable, then normalise

steps.caption: The chain is R → W → S. We observed S = 1 (a skid). We want R (rain). W (wet road) is hidden: neither asked nor observed. For each value of R we add up the joint over every value of W.
These sums are P(R=1, S=1) = 0.110 and P(R=0, S=1) = 0.200. They add to 0.310, not 1, so they are not yet probabilities of R. Divide each by 0.310.
P(R=1 | S=1) = 0.110 ÷ 0.310 = 0.355. The skid raised the chance of rain from the prior 0.2 to 0.355. The two answers 0.355 and 0.645 add to 1.
The chain is X → Y → Z → W with evidence W = 1. We want X. The factors are P(X), P(Y | X), P(Z | Y) and P(W=1 | Z). Eliminate the hidden variables one at a time: Z first, then Y.
Eliminate Z. Only two factors mention Z: P(Z | Y) and P(W=1 | Z). Multiply them and sum Z out. h(Y=1) = 0.6 × 0.9 + 0.4 × 0.1 = 0.58. h(Y=0) = 0.2 × 0.9 + 0.8 × 0.1 = 0.26.
Only X is left. Multiply by its factor P(X) = 0.5: 0.5 × 0.516 = 0.258 and 0.5 × 0.356 = 0.178.
These are P(X, W=1). They add to 0.436, so normalise: 0.258 ÷ 0.436 = 0.592 and 0.178 ÷ 0.436 = 0.408.

scenes.title: Likelihood weighting: fixed evidence, weighted samples

steps.caption: We want P(Y=1 | X=1, Z=1). Likelihood weighting never rejects a sample. It fixes the evidence X = 1 and Z = 1, and samples only Y.
Sample Y from P(Y | X=1). Here P(Y=1 | X=1) = 0.7. Suppose five draws give Y = 1, 0, 1, 1, 0.
Weight each sample by how well it fits the evidence: weight = P(X=1) × P(Z=1 | Y), with P(X=1) = 0.4. If Y = 1: 0.4 × 0.9 = 0.36. If Y = 0: 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12.
Add the weights for each value of Y. Y = 1 has three samples: 3 × 0.36 = 1.08. Y = 0 has two samples: 2 × 0.12 = 0.24.
Estimate P(Y=1 | X=1, Z=1) = 1.08 ÷ (1.08 + 0.24) = 1.08 ÷ 1.32 ≈ 0.818. The exact answer is 0.875. A sampling estimate is close but not exact.

scenes.title: A joint table: marginals, conditionals and Bayes

steps.caption: This is the joint table of flu F and a test T (T = 1 means positive). Each cell is a probability of a combination, and the four cells add to 1.
Marginalise: add across a row to sum out T. P(F=1) = 0.08 + 0.02 = 0.10. P(F=0) = 0.09 + 0.81 = 0.90.
Add down a column to sum out F. P(T=1) = 0.08 + 0.09 = 0.17. P(T=0) = 0.02 + 0.81 = 0.83. The grand total is 1.
Condition: given T = 1, look only at the T = 1 column and rescale it to add to 1. P(F=1 | T=1) = 0.08 ÷ 0.17 ≈ 0.471.
Bayes' rule gives the same number from the other direction. P(T=1 | F=1) = 0.08 ÷ 0.10 = 0.8, so P(F=1 | T=1) = 0.8 × 0.10 ÷ 0.17 ≈ 0.471. The two conditionals differ: 0.8 is not 0.471.
